old_title: Carlos Alcaraz blazes past Frances Tiafoe in ATP Finals tennis group stage - as it happened
new_title: Carlos Alcaraz blazes past Frances Tiafoe in ATP Finals tennis group stage - as it happened
old_text:
Carlos Alcaraz took almost five months off, recovering from a wrist injury, but has returned in typically devastating style, Francis Tiafoe seen off 6-2 6-2 in the opening game of Ivan Lendl Group Though he lost to Ben Shelton at the US Open, his first tournament back, he has won three of the last four and, if he maintains his level, will be almost impossible to beat this week.
Alcaraz was into his stride immediately, breaking in game one then again in game three, Tiafoe - making his debut in this event - struggling to land his first serve and doing little with his second. Consequently, the opening set was over almost before it'd started, Alcaraz racing to a 6-2 lead without even showing the full array of his talent, his drop-shot and net-play largely absent, unrequired.
Tiafoe did improve a little in set two, looking to be more aggressive, but he was broken for 2-1 before spurning three break-back points to go down 4-2. It was no great surprise that, following such disappointment, he was promptly broken a second time, and from there Alcaraz, yet to win this competition, closed out a hugely impressive victory
Tonight in Ivan Lendl Group, Daniil Medvedev, a former winner of this competition, faces Flavio Cobolli, the home favourite. That means pressure for him but the kind of atmosphere that might wind up his opponent, who is famously able to complain bout anything, having groused that his body is packing up and he doesn't want to play tennis. I'm looking forward to it, but indoors, I'm backing Medvedev.
Tiafoe, for his part, knew he was overmatched, looking forlornly at his team with what-can-you-do facials. Ultimately, Alcaraz and Sinner are still way ahead of the rest and, though anyone is beatable in a one-off, it doesn't look like anyone on tour can get good enough to do so regularly in the next couple of years.
The thing about that performance was - well there were various things - but we didn't even see the full ranger of what Alcaraz can do. There was, I think, just one drop shot, and he only came to net once too. Once he's grooved into the competition, he's going to be a tricky proposition.
Alcaraz says he's never felt this energised at this part of the season, which makes sense given the time off. He's never experienced anything like this year, with months off competition, but now he's here with energy and is hungry for more.
He prepared the match tactics really well, started solid to let Tiafoe know if he wants to win it'll be a great battle, and he's really happy to have started the tournament like this. Oh, and that appears to be it.
Tiafoe won't despair: he knows that playing like that, Alcaraz beats everyone, and also that he's settled into the competition and its conditions by losing the match he was least likely to win. He's now able to get after Medvedev and Cobolli, both of whom he can beat, knowing how the court plays.
What a joy it is to watch Alcaraz play, the joy he takes, the joy we take, the joy he takes in our joy, the joy we take in his. He's an absolute genius, and young enough to break pretty much every record worth having if he stays fit and focused.
*Alcaraz 6-2 6-2 Tiafoe Tiafoe sends Alcaraz out wide and the forehand riposte hits the net; 0-15. But then a backhand floats tamely wide, it's soon 30-15, and when the American comes in, a wrong-footing forehand down the line catches him tp raise two match points. And, though this time, Tiafoe picks the serve, moving out wide to return, he frames the shot, and that's that. A sensational performance from Alcaraz, who'll take some beating, while Tiafoe can only laugh; he knows he can't beat that, and that he's now got two more matches, against Medvedev and Cobolli, to try and make the last four.
Alcaraz 6-2 5-2 Tiafoe* I'd not be surprised to see Alcaraz break here, and when a Tiafoe forehand goes wide, he makes 15-all then a fine forehand down the line facilitates another from the opposite corner, this one a winner; 15-30, and Tiafoe looks as helpless as he does befuddled. He does make 30-all, but then, forced to deliver a second serve, finds himself under pressure and swats a backhand wide ... before serving into the net. And have a look! Again, Alcaraz hits beautifully from the back, then tested with a fine backhand from Tiafoe, unleashes a glorious effort os his own, guided down the line to secure a second double-break. After a quick sit-down, he'll be serving for the match; this is ominous, affirming stuff.
*Alcaraz 6-2 4-2 Tiafoe Alcaraz comes in to make a volley below the level of the net, beautifully controlled, for 15-0 then, after a wild first serve, nets a forehand; 15-all. The one-two punch of short serve out wide, clean-up forehand to the opposite corner, makes 30-15, though, then Tiafoe plays a decent point ... until he loses it. Oh, but up 40-15, Alcaraz hauls a forehand wide, then sends another long and, by the standard, this is a chance, the first deuce on the Spaniard's serve, and a backhand down the line but into the net raises break-back point! Who saw that coming? Naturally, a service winner follows, Tiafoe expecting a ball to the fore only for it to arrive at the back ... but another unforced error, a forehand into the net, means a second breaking opportunity. So Alcaraz makes the same serve that saved him last time, again Tiafoe guesses incorrectly, and the ball hits the net. But the level has dropped, Alcaraz perhaps finding it too easy, and a further unforced error means a further break point, the third of the game. This time, the serve does go to the forehand but, when it comes back, a winner down the line restores deuce, and from there, Alcarax closes out, just, Tiafoe again playing an excellent rally only to net when momentum suddenly switches. On the one hand, that was better from him; on the other, it might also have been his chance, from 40-15 to three break points spurned, to another hold.
Alcaraz 6-2 3-2 Tiafoe* Huge hitting from the back makes Tiafoe 15-0, problem being he has to play like that almost every rally - and, as Tim points out in comms, he pulled back a bit on serve, presumably unenthusiastic about a second delivery, given his inability, so far, to win a point that way. But he makes 40-15 with an ace, then another first serve leads to an overhit return. Tiafoe had to win that game and he did, but can he even get close to breaking back?
*Alcaraz 6-2 3-1 Tiafoe This is a seriously chastening experience for Tiafoe, a welcome-to-the-big-leagues tousing. As if to highlight one of the many differences between them, Alcaraz shows how to hit a nasty second serve, backing it up with a winner for 30-0, then whips a violent forehand crosscourt to raise three consolidation points. The first is saved, Tiafoe ordered by his team to "take it to him" - er, easier said than done, lads - then a drop, the first of the match is netted for 40-30. For the first time, Alcaraz is under a modicum of pressure, but a return, just a little long, releases it almost immediately.
Alcaraz 6-2 2-1 Tiafoe* A fine return, close to the line, elicits an error; Tiafoe badly needs the ace with which he makes it 15-all. Still, though, the sense is that he's hanging on, the next rally the longest of the match so far ... and it's Alcaraz who eventually errs. That's big for Big Foe but, sent wide on the backhand, he nets ... then raises fame point with an ace, 10-0 for first serves in this set. But he then has to try a second delivery, ups the pace on it too ... only for Alcaraz to take control of the rally, forcing the error and taking us to deuce. Another rally unfolds, Tiafoe again doing what he has to, increasing the aggression ... but, as a consequence, missing with a forehand that's barely a few inches out of court. Such is the ordeal of facing Alcaraz who, up advantage, climbs into a second serve - Tiafoe is yet to win a point behind one - and, though he doesn't finish the rally when he should, picking the wrong corner to hit at, when he's then picked out at the net, he improvises a cross court lob, and this is five to over.
*Alcaraz 6-2 1-1 Tiafoe But can he make an impression on the Alcaraz serve? Er, no. At 15-0, offered a rare second serve, he doesn't do enough and a winner soon fizzes past; at 30-0 a return goes long; and at 40-0, he's jammed-up by a body serve.
Alcaraz 6-2 0-1 Tiafoe* An unforced error puts Tiafoe under immediate pressure, and he's in a tricky position: foes he take more risks, trying to end points but increasing the margin for error, or does he play safe, allowing Alcaraz to hit winners off rally balls? In this game, he moves closer to the former, winning four points on the spin to lead in set two.
*Alcaraz 6-2 Tiafoe Under pressure to make something happen, Tiafoe forces a forehand - it's wide - then an ace makes 30-0. And, though a devilishly hard and wide second serve offers the chance to hit a winner on return, the gap is tiny, Tiafoe misses it, and a second ace of the game seals a one-sided set, one point lost on serve. Carlos Alcaraz is good at tennis and it's not possible to play that much better than he did there - though he can and no doubt will over the course of the week.
Alcaraz 5-2 Tiafoe* Better from Tiafoe, making 15-0 then coming in - which seems to be a strategy - to put away a fine oblique volley, on the backhand and cross-court. An ace follows, then a long return, so Alcaraz will at least have to serve for the set.
*Alcaraz 5-1 Tiafoe At 15-0, Tiafoe wins his first point on the Alcaraz serve ... for all the good it does him. The world no 2 is playing beautifully, polishing off the game to 15 when, though sent a decent forehand, he responds with a backhand down the line that's far too good.
Alcaraz 4-1 Tiafoe* But this is better from Tiafoe, a forehand winner, his first of the match, backed up by an ace. And it's soon 40-0, though worth noting that, after a fine backhand smash, he was still forced to play a follow-up. But after a forehand winner from Alcaraz, he sees out the hold, saluting the crowd in exhibition self-mockery; he's in the match.
*Alcaraz 4-0 Tiafoe Alcaraz is the kindliest assassin since Leon, but an assassin nonetheless. He holds to love, Tiafoe having won just five points in the match so far, and the crowd try to get him going; to a top pro, that'll be slightly embarrassing.
Alcaraz 3-0 Tiafoe* Tiafoe comes in off a forehand, another shot that doesn't ask enough of his opponent, but the response goes long ... then so too does a forehand which takes us to 15-all. Alcaraz is crushing it from the back, allowing no time for adjustment, and when Tiafoe comes in again, this time he's passed with a dipping forehand; that's five winners already. And, well, gosh: more thwacking from the back, another forehand winner, and two points for a double break. Tiafoe, though, lands first serve - he's missed too many of those already - then plays a better rally for 30-40, only for Alcaraz to unfurl that forehand once more, yet another winner securing another break. We said that to win, the American needed to start well, and, um, he hasn't.
*Alcaraz 2-0 Tiafoe I wonder if Tiafoe was nervous; he didn't seem to unload in his shots in that game, while Alcaraz was right into stroke, and he consolidates to love, sealing the deal with a booming ace out wide. Up goes the pressure...
Alcaraz 1-0 Tiafoe* (*denotes server) Tiafoe overhits a forehand, but levels the game when a return floats long ... then another, but a double takes us to 30-all. Then, at 40-30, the first proper point of the match, Alcaraz sending backhands to opposite corners, the first inside-out and second down the line, a winner; deuce. Oh, and another winner, a forehand hooked cross after Tiafoe doesn't do enough with one of his own, raises break point ... converted when a flat forehand incites a netted riposte. Exactly the start the underdog didn't need.
We're now watching Tiafoe give an interview to Sky after the pre-tournament photoshoot; he's forgotten to remove his shades, perhaps the reason his shirt collar is skew-whiff. Ah well.
So where is the game? Alcaraz will do his usual thing, looking to unleash that forehand; Tiafoe will look to target the backhand, keep him moving, and perhaps deny him pace while varying angles. He'll also want to go for his shots, because the longer the rallies go, the more chances Alcaraz will have to finish them.
So to Alcaraz and Tiafoe, who've met three times. Tiafoe won the first, on clay, Alcaraz the other two, five-setters at Flushing Meadow and Wimbkedon, which is to say he knows he can compete against the favourite on equal terms.
I wonder if, as Andreeva develops, she works out how not to miss against Gauff - my sense is she does - and I'd fancy her against Rybakina on clay. But can she find a way of handling bigger and better athletes?
This is what Coach Calv said about her in the summer:
Andreeva is just a beautiful tennis player. She times the ball so clean that if she's on and the other player isn't, it can seem like there's no way to beat her.
To which I'd add that she's a killer. She expects to win majors, handles pressure, and is still improving in all aspects. I agree there'll be times she's hit through, but increasingly, opponents will know that to beat her, they need to be at or close to their best because her bottom and modal levels are stratospheric. That's intimidating stuff.
I asked Calvin Betton, our resident coach, and he replied thusly:
She's a very good tennis player, but lacks firepower against Rybakina and Gauff for different reasons. Rybakina can straight up overpower her, Gauff just makes her miss, and you also have to imagine Swiatek comes again. She'll win matches and be at the top of the game, but not enough to dominate I don't think.
Before we dig further into our afternoon's entertainment, what the women's event? Mirra Andreeva might just be over a hump, winning her first slam at Roland Garros and now taking this title, without losing a set; is she on her way to becoming the best player in the world?
It was hard not to feel some level of relief when Carlos Alcaraz lost a five-set epic to Ben Shelton at the US Open because, after missing almost five months and two majors with what must've been a fairly significant wrist injury, for him to immediately reassert by taking his first tournament back, despite not being at full power, would not have spoken well of the game.
On the other hand, he has important and pressing tennising to do; while he was away and settling back in, Jannik Sinner unwell in Paris, hurt his knee at Wimbledon and took the rest of the year off to recover. This left a power vacuum at the top of the men's game which Alexander Zverev, hitherto unable to snaffle a big pot, has exploited; he now holds two of the four slams having beaten neither of the top two in either while winning nothing else all year, also not what the game needs.
Alcaraz, though, is nearing his best form, 20-2 since his return having won Japan, Vienna and Paris, which his to say it'll take something proper to stop him here. But Francis Tiafoe is capable. Several years ago now, a coach messaged me to say he'd seen someone special - the teenage Big Foe - and though he's not quite delivered on his promise, he's recently reunited with Mark Kovacs, his head coach, and looked a different, more assertive player at the US Open, when he lost to Shelton in the semis.
Since then, though, he's struggled, returning two first-round and two second-round defeats in the four tournaments he's played. It feels unlikely that, in such context, he'll suddenly hit the kind of level he needs to beat the best in the world, but he loves the big occasion and, making his debut in this competition, will arrive with a plan and commit to attack. If he starts well, he's a chance.
